A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same 3MDBench study. Their main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v2 reports original patient/assessor selection experiments, diagnostic and clinical-competence evaluations, temperament analyses, and convolutional-model comparisons.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and reports additional Gemma/MedGemma evaluations, human complaint validation, and physician diagnostic comparisons.

M1.justification: The agent architecture, selected Patient and Assessor Agents, six diagnostic strategies, and top-three EfficientNetV2-XL cue integration remain unchanged. Matching v2 Appendix F with v3 Appendix H reveals minor prompt corrections, including the assessor criterion reference, rather than a new procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same 34 diagnoses, five medical domains, English multimodal consultations, and four patient temperaments. The human studies use existing cases and retained information conditions; revised sample counts do not establish new clinical coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 5–6 add MedGemma-4B, MedGemma-27B, and Gemma3-27B alongside the retained doctor models, enabling specialized-versus-general comparisons. New Table 7 also compares GPT-4o-mini with four physicians under matched information conditions. Patient, assessor, and EfficientNet comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Reported test/train/validation sizes change from 3,013/2,424/606 to 2,996/2,396/596. v3 also introduces a 34-case physician/model pilot with different physician pairs assigned to minimal- and full-information conditions. The main dialogue cap, temperatures, and token budgets remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v2's general statements about manual checks, v3 Appendix C reports structured human assessments of basic-complaint relevance and additional complaints' diagnostic and visual relevance. Figure 13 adds criterion-level clinical-competence analysis by disease category, and Appendix J replaces the melancholic eczema example. Existing prompting, temperament, and confusion-matrix analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Utterance counts by diagnosis change from mean/error-bar panels in v2 Figure 10 to boxplots showing distributional summaries and outliers in v3 Figure 11. Appendix B removes the repeated-task self-agreement statistic. Wilcoxon testing and Benjamini–Hochberg correction remain unchanged, with no newly documented run or seed counts.

E6.justification: Table 5 adds dialogue-plus-image F1 scores of 37.9, 45.7, and 51.1 for MedGemma-4B, MedGemma-27B, and Gemma3-27B, respectively; retained model rows are unchanged. Appendix C adds 88%/92% complaint-relevance approval rates, and Table 7 adds separate pilot results, including full-information F1 of 54.55 for GPT-4o-mini versus physicians' 57.58 and 54.55. Reported human agreement changes from 0.48 to 0.49. v3 Figure 10 also displays identical competence bars across models, unlike the model-specific criterion-4.1 results in v2 Figure 11.

T1.justification: The scenario notation and mathematical substance of the framework remain unchanged. Neither version provides theoretical results or proofs that are added, removed, or revised.

C1.justification: v3 explicitly positions naturally completed consultations as a distinguishing capability, criticizing artificial dialogue interruptions in prior benchmarks. The principal benchmark contributions and headline claims of 6.5% and up-to-20% F1 improvements remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 adds a proposed specialist-imaging bias explanation for MedGemma's weaker telemedicine performance and interprets the human pilot as suggesting physician-comparable performance with complete information. Section 4.3 replaces v2's overly broad competence summary with model-specific qualifications and discussion of ceiling effects. Limitations more explicitly address single-diagnosis, fixed-label evaluation and possible open-ended alternatives.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the anonymous code pointer with a named GitHub repository and specifies image-quality checks involving size, blur, and watermarks. It also documents human-study qualifications, forms, and assessment procedures. Existing inference settings, hardware disclosures, and convolutional-model training descriptions are largely retained.

R1.justification: Table 1 adds comparison rows for MTMedDialog, AgentClinic, MedAgentSim, AI Hospital, and Dr.APP, together with a full-consultation-completion column. Related work consequently sharpens the benchmark's positioning around combined capabilities. Section 3.5 replaces the medical-model availability rationale with direct positioning against medically specialized models.

P1.justification: v3 makes targeted rewrites and condensations in the introduction, patient-metric descriptions, results discussion, and limitations, and adds two human-evaluation appendix sections. Author affiliations and contact information also change. The main section sequence and most prompt-appendix text remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 2 expands to include an annotated consultation example; several bar charts become heatmaps, radar charts, or boxplots; and Figure 7 becomes a nested-ring display. Table 1 gains a comparison dimension, Tables 5–6 and appendix panels expand, and a human-comparison table is added. The diagnosis confusion matrices are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: The added medical-model comparisons and human studies address v2's limited validation, while the revised competence discussion corrects an overgeneralization. However, v3 Figure 10 replaces differing model-specific competence results with identical bars, and Appendix C describes approval by at least one physician as inter-rater agreement. Together with unexplained dataset-count revisions, these reporting problems make the net quality benefit uncertain despite the useful additions.
